opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So DecodingTrust really came out of a sense that the way we were evaluating language models was too narrow. A lot of the benchmarks at the time focused on capability, things like accuracy on question answering or reasoning tasks, and trustworthiness was often treated as an afterthought or reduced to a single dimension, maybe toxicity or maybe bias in isolation.

What we tried to do was step back and ask: if you're actually going to deploy one of these models in a setting where people depend on it, what are all the ways it could let you down? We ended up organizing the evaluation around several perspectives: toxicity, stereotype bias, adversarial robustness, out-of-distribution robustness, robustness to adversarial demonstrations in context, privacy, machine ethics, and fairness. The idea is that trustworthiness is multidimensional, and a model can look great on one axis and be quite fragile on another.

One of the findings I think was most interesting, and maybe a little counterintuitive, was that the more capable models, the ones that were better at following instructions, could also be more vulnerable in certain ways. If you give them misleading system prompts or carefully crafted jailbreaking instructions, their very ability to follow instructions faithfully makes them easier to push into producing toxic or biased content, or leaking private information. So capability and trustworthiness don't necessarily move together, and sometimes there's real tension between them.

In terms of its role, I see it as one piece of a broader ecosystem. It's not meant to be the final word on whether a model is safe. It's more of a diagnostic tool, a way to surface failure modes systematically so developers, researchers, and ideally policymakers have a shared vocabulary and a shared set of tests. We released it openly precisely so people could build on it, extend it, and hold models accountable over time.

And I'd add that evaluation itself is a scientific problem we're still figuring out. Benchmarks can saturate, models can be trained in ways that game them, and the contexts where these systems get deployed keep changing. So part of what I hope DecodingTrust contributes is not just the specific numbers, but a way of thinking about evaluation that's more holistic and more honest about where these models still fall short.

r001.rationale: The response describes DecodingTrust as evaluating multiple distinct trustworthiness dimensions, including toxicity, bias, robustness, privacy, ethics, and fairness.

r002.rationale: It says existing benchmarks focused on capability measures such as question answering and reasoning, while trustworthiness was often an afterthought, which DecodingTrust addresses.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about DecodingTrust is that when GPT-4 and these other models started landing, everyone was running them through capability benchmarks, but almost no one was asking a structured, comprehensive question about whether you could actually trust them. There were isolated studies on toxicity, or on bias, or on privacy, but they weren't talking to each other, and they weren't being run on the same models under the same conditions.

So what we tried to do was build a unified evaluation framework that looks at trustworthiness across multiple dimensions at once. We ended up with eight perspectives: toxicity, stereotype bias, adversarial robustness, out-of-distribution robustness, robustness to adversarial demonstrations in the prompt, privacy, machine ethics, and fairness. And within each one, we don't just run a single benchmark. We design scenarios that probe how the model behaves under pressure. Benign prompts, adversarial system prompts, jailbreak-style instructions, few-shot examples that are deliberately misleading, and so on.

The reason that matters is that a model can look great on a standard test and fall over the moment someone nudges it. One of the findings that surprised people was that GPT-4 was often more trustworthy than GPT-3.5 on the standard benchmarks, but it was also more vulnerable to certain adversarial system prompts and misleading demonstrations, presumably because it follows instructions more faithfully. So being better at the task and being more trustworthy are not the same axis, and DecodingTrust is really an attempt to make that second axis measurable.

I'd also say its role is partly about shifting norms. Once you have a public framework, a leaderboard, and open code, it becomes much harder for a model developer to say "we're safe" without pointing at something concrete. Companies started running DecodingTrust internally, regulators and policy folks started referencing it, and that pushes trustworthiness from a vague aspiration into something you can track over time and compare across models.

That said, I try to be honest about its limits. It's a snapshot of what we knew how to measure at a particular moment. Trustworthiness is context dependent, the threat landscape shifts, and models can be tuned against any fixed benchmark. So I see DecodingTrust less as a final verdict and more as scaffolding for an ongoing practice, where the community keeps adding perspectives, updating scenarios, and asking harder questions as these systems get deployed in higher-stakes settings.

r001.rationale: The response describes a unified framework that measures trustworthiness across eight distinct perspectives, including toxicity, bias, robustness, privacy, ethics, and fairness.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the prevalence of capability benchmarks with the lack of structured, comprehensive trustworthiness evaluation, presenting DecodingTrust as addressing that gap.

astra-6.text:
I think of DecodingTrust as a way to make trustworthiness more concrete and measurable. A model can be very capable on a standard benchmark, but that doesn’t tell you whether it will behave reliably when the input changes, whether it exposes private information, or whether its responses are biased. Those are different questions, and we need evaluations that distinguish them.

The goal isn’t to give a model a single score and declare it trustworthy. It’s to understand where it performs well, where it fails, and under what conditions those failures emerge. That can help developers improve models and help people deploying them decide which additional safeguards they need.

And I’d emphasize that this is an ongoing process. An evaluation gives you evidence about the conditions you tested; it doesn’t establish trustworthiness for every possible use. So I see DecodingTrust as a foundation for more systematic scrutiny, with evaluations that evolve alongside the models and the ways people use them.

r001.rationale: The response describes making trustworthiness concrete and measurable by evaluating distinct concerns: reliability under changed inputs, privacy exposure, and bias.

r002.rationale: It contrasts standard capability benchmarks with trustworthiness questions those benchmarks do not answer, identifying a gap in performance-focused evaluation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of DecodingTrust as a way to make trustworthiness more concrete. When we say a language model is trustworthy, what do we actually mean? We might care about toxicity, bias, privacy, robustness, or whether it behaves fairly. Those are different properties, and doing well on one doesn’t necessarily mean doing well on the others.

So the role of the benchmark is to evaluate those dimensions systematically and understand where models fail, including when someone deliberately tries to get them to behave badly. A model can look very good under a standard prompt and behave quite differently when you change the context or introduce an adversarial instruction.

I wouldn’t interpret the results as a certificate that a model is safe. They’re a diagnostic: they help researchers identify weaknesses and give people deploying these systems a more informed starting point. You still need to evaluate the model in the context where you’re actually going to use it.

r001.rationale: The response makes trustworthiness concrete by evaluating distinct dimensions such as toxicity, bias, privacy, robustness, and fairness.

r002.rationale: It describes DecodingTrust’s diagnostic role, but does not identify a gap in existing work focused on language-model performance evaluation.
